subject: Medicine
topic: Myxedema Coma Resuscitation and Hydrocortisone Preceding Levothyroxine
stem: An 81-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance in mid-January after being found unresponsive in her unheated apartment. Her past medical history is notable for Hashimoto thyroiditis, for which she was prescribed levothyroxine; however, neighbors report she stopped filling her prescriptions 6 months ago. On physical examination, she is comatose and unarousable to noxious stimuli. Physical examination reveals cool, dry, rough skin with coarse sparse hair, prominent periorbital non-pitting edema, and delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes. Vital signs are: rectal temperature 33.4 C (92.1 F), pulse 42/min and regular, blood pressure 82/50 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 8/min with shallow respiratory excursions. Cardiac monitoring confirms sinus bradycardia without ischemic ST changes. Fingerstick blood glucose is 54 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas on room air reveals: pH 7.24, PaCO2 62 mm Hg, PaO2 56 mm Hg, and HCO3 26 mEq/L (severe hypercapnic hypoventilation). Serum sodium is 124 mEq/L. Blood is drawn for emergent laboratory testing including serum TSH, free T4, and baseline cortisol. Endotracheal intubation is performed for airway protection. Which of the following pharmacotherapeutic interventions is the most critical immediate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous stress-dose hydrocortisone administered prior to or concurrently with intravenous levothyroxine and liothyronine
options.explanation: This patient presents with MYXEDEMA COMA, an extreme, life-threatening manifestation of decompensated hypothyroidism with a historical mortality rate of 30% to 50%. It typically occurs in elderly patients with longstanding untreated hypothyroidism exposed to secondary precipitants such as hypothermia, sepsis, myocardial infarction, or sedative medications. Diagnostic hallmarks include the combination of: (1) Altered mental status (lethargy, obtundation, or coma); (2) Defective thermoregulation leading to severe hypothermia (core temperature < 35 C / 95 F); (3) Severe cardiopulmonary depression (sinus bradycardia, hypotension, and respiratory depression with hypoxemia and hypercapnic respiratory acidosis); (4) Hyponatremia (due to impaired free-water clearance from low cardiac output and elevated vasopressin) and hypoglycemia; and (5) Physical stigmata of severe hypothyroidism (periorbital puffiness, non-pitting pretibial myxedema, and delayed reflex relaxation). MANDATORY RESUSCITATION PRINCIPLE: According to American Thyroid Association guidelines, INTRAVENOUS STRESS-DOSE GLUCOCORTICOIDS (hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 hours) MUST BE ADMINISTERED PRIOR TO OR CONCURRENTLY WITH INTRAVENOUS THYROID HORMONE REPLACEMENT (IV levothyroxine with or without IV liothyronine). RATIONALE: Thyroid hormone profoundly increases cellular metabolic activity and accelerates the hepatic breakdown and peripheral clearance of circulating cortisol. In patients with severe myxedema coma, the clinician cannot immediately exclude concomitant primary adrenal insufficiency (such as autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2) or secondary adrenal insufficiency from hypothalamic-pituitary failure. Administering thyroid hormone monotherapy without prior corticosteroid coverage accelerates cortisol degradation, precipitating catastrophic, irreversible circulatory collapse and fatal ACUTE ADRENAL CRISIS.

options.text: Intravenous levothyroxine monotherapy bolus, withholding glucocorticoids until serum cortisol results are finalized 4 hours later
options.explanation: Withholding glucocorticoids until laboratory results return can cause fatal circulatory collapse if thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol clearance in an adrenal-deficient patient.

options.text: Immediate active external rewarming with convective forced-air blankets and hot water immersion
options.explanation: Active aggressive external rewarming causes sudden peripheral cutaneous vasodilation, resulting in severe intravascular pooling and refractory hypovolemic shock; passive rewarming is indicated.

options.text: Rapid infusion of 3 liters of 0.9% normal saline over 1 hour to aggressively treat hypotension and hyponatremia
options.explanation: Rapid fluid loading in myxedema coma precipitates acute pulmonary edema and cerebral demyelination; cautious, slow crystalloid infusion is required.

options.text: Intravenous dopamine infusion as first-line inotropic therapy to restore normal heart rate and blood pressure
options.explanation: Dopamine is ineffective in correcting hypothermia-induced bradycardia and worsens myocardial oxygen demand; thyroid hormone and glucocorticoids restore hemodynamics.

topic: Thyroid Storm Multimodal Medical Therapy and Potassium Iodide Timing
stem: A 34-year-old woman with a history of Graves disease who was lost to follow-up and non-compliant with methimazole presents to the emergency department with acute delirium, severe agitation, profuse sweating, and palpitations that began 12 hours ago after developing acute pyelonephritis. On physical examination, she is combative, disoriented, and profusely diaphoretic. Vital signs are: temperature 40.2 C (104.4 F), pulse 154/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 168/74 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 28/min. Physical examination demonstrates bilateral exophthalmos, a diffusely enlarged nontender thyroid gland with an audible systolic bruit, elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral bibasilar crackles, and marked tremor. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale score is calculated at 65 points (diagnostic of thyroid storm). Point-of-care laboratory tests confirm suppressed TSH (< 0.01 microU/mL) and free T4 markedly elevated (> 7.0 ng/dL). The intensive care team establishes intravenous access to initiate multimodal pharmacotherapy. Which of the following sequences represents the most appropriate, guideline-adherent pharmacological strategy for this patient?

options.text: Administer potassium iodide solution immediately as first-line therapy, followed by oral propylthiouracil 2 hours later, and avoid beta-blockers due to atrial fibrillation
options.explanation: Giving iodine before PTU fuels synthesis of new thyroid hormones; beta-blockers are the cornerstone of rate control in thyroid storm-induced atrial fibrillation.

options.text: Initiate intravenous propranolol, administer oral or rectal propylthiouracil, delay potassium iodide administration until at least 1 hour after propylthiouracil, and administer intravenous hydrocortisone
options.explanation: This patient presents with fulminant THYROID STORM (accelerated thyrotoxicosis), an endocrine emergency triggered by acute pyelonephritis in the setting of untreated Graves disease. The clinical diagnosis is established using the Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (score >= 45 is diagnostic), characterized by severe hyperpyrexia, cardiovascular collapse (tachyarrhythmias, atrial fibrillation, high-output heart failure), central nervous system agitation/delirium, and gastrointestinal-hepatic dysfunction (jaundice, diarrhea). MANAGEMENT ALGORITHM AND CRITICAL TIMING SEQUENCE: Management mandates a simultaneous, four-pronged therapeutic approach: (1) BETA-ADRENERGIC BLOCKADE: High-dose intravenous or oral PROPRANOLOL (or IV esmolol) is initiated immediately to control adrenergic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, tremor) and reduce myocardial oxygen demand. Propranolol has the additional unique benefit of inhibiting peripheral 5'-monodeiodinase, blocking the conversion of T4 to active T3. (2) THIONAMIDE THERAPY: PROPYLTHIOURACIL (PTU) is the thionamide of choice in acute thyroid storm (administered orally, via nasogastric tube, or rectally). PTU acts via two mechanisms: it inhibits thyroid peroxidase (blocking new organification and coupling of thyroid hormones) and directly inhibits peripheral deiodination of T4 to T3 (methimazole only blocks thyroid peroxidase, though it can be used if PTU is unavailable). (3) INORGANIC IODINE SOLUTION (SSKI or Lugol solution): Inorganic iodine induces the WOLFF-CHAIKOFF EFFECT, acutely shutting down the release of preformed T4 and T3 from the thyroid follicular lumen into the bloodstream. CRITICAL TIMING RULE: IODINE MUST BE ADMINISTERED AT LEAST 1 HOUR AFTER THE THIONAMIDE DOSE! If inorganic iodine is administered prior to or concurrently with thionamides, the unblocked thyroid gland uses the massive exogenous iodine load as substrate to synthesize and release an explosive new wave of thyroid hormones (the Jod-Basedow phenomenon), precipitating cardiovascular collapse. (4) CORTICOSTEROIDS: Intravenous HYDROCORTISONE (100 mg IV every 8 hours) further blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, stabilizes vasomotor tone, and treats relative adrenal insufficiency induced by hypermetabolic cortisol consumption.

options.text: Initiate high-dose oral aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) for antipyresis, followed by intravenous methimazole and oral potassium iodide simultaneously
options.explanation: Aspirin is strictly contraindicated in thyroid storm because it displaces T4 and T3 from thyroid-binding globulin (TBG), sharply increasing free active hormone levels.

options.text: Perform emergent total thyroidectomy in the operating room under general anesthesia prior to medical stabilization
options.explanation: Emergency thyroidectomy in an unstabilized patient with thyroid storm carries prohibitive intraoperative mortality (>50%); medical stabilization is mandatory.

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous levothyroxine to induce negative feedback suppression of the anterior pituitary gland
options.explanation: Administering levothyroxine adds exogenous thyroid hormone to a patient already in hyperthyroid crisis, causing fatal ventricular fibrillation.

topic: Diabetic Ketoacidosis Potassium Repletion and Insulin Timing Thresholds
stem: A 23-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department with nausea, recurrent vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and rapid deep breathing for 24 hours. He ran out of insulin 3 days ago. On physical examination, he appears severely dehydrated with sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, and a fruity odor on his breath. Vital signs are: temperature 37.1 C, pulse 122/min, blood pressure 94/58 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 32/min (Kussmaul breathing). Point-of-care fingerstick glucose reads 'HIGH' (> 500 mg/dL). Laboratory testing reveals: - Serum Sodium: 132 mEq/L - Serum Potassium: 3.1 mEq/L - Serum Chloride: 96 mEq/L - Serum Bicarbonate: 10 mEq/L - Blood Urea Nitrogen: 38 mg/dL - Serum Creatinine: 1.8 mg/dL - Arterial Blood Gas: pH 7.18, PaCO2 24 mm Hg, PaO2 96 mm Hg - Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate: 7.8 mmol/L (normal: < 0.5 mmol/L) - Urine Dipstick: 4+ glucose, large ketones The patient is initiated on intravenous 0.9% normal saline at 1,000 mL/hr. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding insulin and potassium management for this patient?

options.text: Administer an immediate intravenous bolus of regular insulin (0.14 units/kg) to suppress hepatic ketoacid generation rapidly
options.explanation: Giving insulin with a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L drives potassium into cells, causing lethal cardiac arrhythmias and arrest.

options.text: Administer two ampules of intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct arterial pH before giving potassium or insulin
options.explanation: Bicarbonate is indicated only for pH < 6.9; routine bicarbonate causes paradoxical CSF acidosis, hypokalemia, and delayed ketone clearance.

options.text: Withhold insulin administration, aggressively infuse intravenous potassium chloride until serum potassium exceeds 3.3 mEq/L, and only then initiate the regular insulin infusion
options.explanation: This patient presents with classic DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS (DKA), characterized by hyperglycemia, high anion gap metabolic acidosis (anion gap = 132 - [96 + 10] = 26 mEq/L), elevated serum beta-hydroxybutyrate, and Kussmaul respirations. The most critical management rule tested on USMLE Step 2 CK involves POTASSIUM THRESHOLDS PRIOR TO INSULIN ADMINISTRATION: (1) TOTAL BODY POTASSIUM DEPLETION: Although initial serum potassium measurements in DKA are often normal or elevated due to extracellular shifts driven by hyperosmolality, insulin deficiency, and acidosis, ALL patients with DKA suffer profound TOTAL BODY POTASSIUM DEFICITS (typically 300 to 600 mEq) resulting from protracted osmotic diuresis, urinary ketoacid salt wasting, and vomiting. (2) THE SERUM POTASSIUM SAFETY RULE (ADA GUIDELINES): Insulin stimulates the sodium-potassium ATPase pump (Na+/K+-ATPase), driving extracellular potassium rapidly into cells. (a) IF SERUM POTASSIUM IS < 3.3 mEq/L: INSULIN MUST BE WITHHELD! Administer aggressive intravenous potassium chloride (20 to 40 mEq/hr) in isotonic saline until serum potassium rises above 3.3 mEq/L. Initiating insulin while serum potassium is < 3.3 mEq/L causes a catastrophic drop in extracellular potassium, precipitating fatal cardiac arrhythmias (ventricular fibrillation, torsades de pointes, asystole) and respiratory muscle paralysis. (b) IF SERUM POTASSIUM IS 3.3 TO 5.3 mEq/L: Start the intravenous regular insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/hr) AND concurrently infuse 20 to 30 mEq of potassium chloride per liter of intravenous fluids to maintain potassium between 4.0 and 5.0 mEq/L. (c) IF SERUM POTASSIUM IS > 5.3 mEq/L: Start insulin infusion without potassium; recheck potassium levels every 2 hours. (3) DEXTROSE AND ANION GAP CLOSURE: When serum glucose drops to <= 200 mg/dL, add 5% dextrose to fluids to prevent hypoglycemia while CONTINUING INSULIN until the anion gap closes (anion gap <= 12 and serum bicarbonate >= 18 mEq/L).

options.text: Initiate continuous subcutaneous insulin glargine and discharge to the medical floor once blood glucose drops below 250 mg/dL
options.explanation: Severe DKA requires continuous IV regular insulin in an ICU/monitored stepdown setting until the anion gap closes, not floor subcutaneous therapy.

options.text: Discontinue intravenous insulin completely as soon as blood glucose reaches 200 mg/dL to prevent iatrogenic hypoglycemia
options.explanation: Stopping insulin when glucose reaches 200 mg/dL causes rebound ketoacidosis; insulin must be continued with dextrose until the anion gap closes.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to the ambulatory clinic with a 4-month history of worsening fatigue, weakness, dizzy spells upon standing, anorexia, salt cravings, and a 6-kg unintended weight loss. Her medical history includes vitiligo and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. On physical examination, she appears frail and chronical ill. Vital signs are: pulse 88/min, supine blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg, and standing blood pressure 82/48 mm Hg with dizziness (marked orthostatic hypotension). Examination of the skin demonstrates dark, bronze hyperpigmentation of the gingival mucosa, vermilion border of the lips, palmar creases, and old appendectomy scar. Laboratory evaluation reveals: - Serum Sodium: 128 mEq/L - Serum Potassium: 5.8 mEq/L - Serum Chloride: 98 mEq/L - Serum Bicarbonate: 18 mEq/L - Blood Urea Nitrogen: 28 mg/dL - Serum Creatinine: 1.2 mg/dL - Fasting Blood Glucose: 64 mg/dL An 8:00 AM baseline serum cortisol is 2.8 mcg/dL (normal: 5-25 mcg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test to confirm the diagnosis, and what is the definitive immediate maintenance therapy?

options.text: Overnight 1-mg low-dose dexamethasone suppression test; treatment requires oral spironolactone and sodium polystyrene sulfonate
options.explanation: Dexamethasone suppression tests screen for hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome); spironolactone blocks aldosterone and would worsen fatal shock.

options.text: Metyrapone stimulation test; treatment requires oral hydrocortisone monotherapy without mineralocorticoid replacement
options.explanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency destroys the zona glomerulosa and requires fludrocortisone; hydrocortisone monotherapy treats secondary adrenal failure.

options.text: Insulin-induced hypoglycemia test; treatment requires bilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy
options.explanation: Insulin tolerance test assesses pituitary GH/ACTH reserve, but is dangerous in adrenal crisis; adrenalectomy is contraindicated.

options.text: High-dose cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH) stimulation test demonstrating failure of serum cortisol to rise above 18 mcg/dL; treatment requires daily oral hydrocortisone combined with fludrocortisone
options.explanation: This patient presents with classic PRIMARY ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY (Addison disease), likely autoimmune adrenalitis in the setting of Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome type 2 (given her concurrent vitiligo and Hashimoto thyroiditis). Master the key pathophysiological and diagnostic principles on USMLE Step 2 CK: (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF PRIMARY VS SECONDARY ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY: Primary adrenal failure involves autoimmune destruction of all three zones of the adrenal cortex: (a) Zona glomerulosa destruction leads to ALDOSTERONE DEFICIENCY. Loss of aldosterone results in urinary sodium wasting, hypovolemia, orthostatic hypotension, salt craving, HYPONATREMIA, HYPERKALEMIA, and non-anion gap metabolic acidosis (retention of K+ and H+). (b) Zona fasciculata destruction causes CORTISOL DEFICIENCY, leading to fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, and fasting hypoglycemia. (c) Loss of negative feedback inhibition triggers massive pituitary secretion of PRO-OPIOMELANOCORTIN (POMC), the precursor for both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH). Elevated MSH/ACTH stimulates melanocortin-1 receptors on dermal melanocytes, producing pathognomonic BRONZE HYPERPIGMENTATION of mucous membranes, palmar creases, and sun-exposed areas. IN CONTRAST, secondary adrenal insufficiency (pituitary ACTH failure) spares the zona glomerulosa (aldosterone is regulated by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, not ACTH); therefore, patients with secondary adrenal failure DO NOT have hyperkalemia or hyperpigmentation. (2) CONFIRMATORY TESTING: The definitive gold-standard diagnostic test is the COSYNTROPIN (SYNTHETIC ACTH1-24) STIMULATION TEST. Cosyntropin (250 mcg IV or IM) is administered, and serum cortisol is measured at baseline, 30, and 60 minutes. A normal adrenal cortex responds with robust steroidogenesis, yielding a peak cortisol > 18 to 20 mcg/dL. In primary adrenal insufficiency, the atrophic or destroyed adrenal cortex FAILS TO RESPOND (peak cortisol remains < 18 mcg/dL). Baseline plasma ACTH is markedly elevated (> 100 pg/mL). (3) DEFINITIVE MAINTENANCE THERAPY: Because both cortisol and aldosterone are deficient, patients require lifelong replacement with both a glucocorticoid (ORAL HYDROCORTISONE in divided doses) AND a mineralocorticoid (ORAL FLUDROCORTISONE 0.05 to 0.1 mg daily).

options.text: 24-hour urinary free cortisol excretion; treatment requires long-acting somatostatin receptor ligands (octreotide)
options.explanation: Urinary free cortisol tests for Cushing syndrome; octreotide treats acromegaly and carcinoid tumors, not adrenal insufficiency.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the clinic due to recurrent, abrupt episodes of severe throbbing headaches, profuse sweating, facial pallor, and intense heart palpitations that occur two to three times per week. The episodes typically last 15 to 30 minutes and resolve spontaneously, leaving him feeling utterly exhausted. Between episodes, he is asymptomatic. On physical examination, his heart rate is 114/min and regular, and his blood pressure is 196/112 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination demonstrates bilateral arteriolar narrowing without papilledema. Diagnostic evaluation reveals: - Plasma free metanephrines: 4.8 nmol/L (normal: < 0.5 nmol/L) - Plasma free normetanephrines: 8.2 nmol/L (normal: < 0.9 nmol/L) - 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines: Markedly elevated An intravenous contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan reveals a 4.5-cm, well-circumscribed, heterogeneous, lipid-poor vascular mass in the right adrenal medulla. The surgical team schedules the patient for laparoscopic right adrenalectomy in 2 weeks. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacological management sequence to prepare this patient safely for surgery?

options.text: Initiate oral metoprolol succinate monotherapy immediately to control tachycardia, and initiate phenoxybenzamine 24 hours prior to surgery
options.explanation: Administering a beta-blocker before an alpha-blocker results in unopposed alpha-1 vasoconstriction, precipitating catastrophic hypertensive crisis and pulmonary edema.

options.text: Proceed immediately to laparoscopic adrenalectomy within 24 hours without preoperative adrenergic blockade to avoid surgical delay
options.explanation: Operating without preoperative blockade carries a perioperative mortality > 30% from intraoperative catecholamine storms triggering fatal hypertensive crisis.

options.text: Prescribe oral spironolactone plus lisinopril to block mineralocorticoid receptors and angiotensin-converting enzyme
options.explanation: Spironolactone and ACE inhibitors do not block alpha-adrenergic receptors and provide zero protection against catecholamine-induced intraoperative surges.

options.text: Initiate high-dose intravenous nitroprusside infusion for 14 days followed by oral atenolol monotherapy
options.explanation: Nitroprusside is used for acute hypertensive crises, not outpatient preoperative preparation; atenolol alone causes unopposed alpha stimulation.

options.text: Initiate oral phenoxybenzamine 10 to 14 days preoperatively, optimize intravascular volume with a high-sodium diet, and add a beta-blocker only after achieving adequate alpha-blockade
options.explanation: This patient presents with the classic clinical triad of PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA (episodic headache, profuse diaphoresis, and palpitations/tachycardia accompanied by paroxysmal hypertension). Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine-secreting neuroendocrine tumors derived from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla (secreting norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine). PREOPERATIVE PHARMACOLOGICAL MANAGEMENT (ENDOCRINE SOCIETY GUIDELINES): Complete surgical resection (laparoscopic adrenalectomy) is the definitive cure. However, intraoperative tumor manipulation can trigger massive, lethal catecholamine surges. Therefore, RIGOROUS PREOPERATIVE MEDICAL PREPARATION IS MANDATORY: (1) STEP 1: ALPHA-ADRENERGIC BLOCKADE FIRST: Preoperative preparation begins 10 to 14 days prior to surgery with an alpha-adrenergic receptor antagonist. The traditional agent of choice is PHENOXYBENZAMINE, an irreversible, non-selective, non-competitive alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptor blocker. (Selective alpha-1 blockers like doxazosin, prazosin, or terazosin are acceptable alternatives with fewer side effects). Phenoxybenzamine blocks vascular smooth muscle alpha-1 receptors, reversing intense vasoconstriction, normalizing blood pressure, and expanding the contracted intravascular plasma volume. (2) STEP 2: HIGH-SALT DIET AND VOLUME EXPANSION: Chronic catecholamine-induced vasoconstriction produces severe intravascular volume contraction. Once alpha-blockade is established, patients must be encouraged to consume a high-sodium diet and generous oral fluids to restore effective circulatory volume and prevent catastrophic refractory orthostatic hypotension upon operative tumor excision. (3) STEP 3: BETA-BLOCKADE ONLY AFTER ADEQUATE ALPHA-BLOCKADE: A beta-adrenergic antagonist (such as propranolol or atenolol) is added 2 to 3 days preoperatively to manage reflex tachycardia or catecholamine-induced tachyarrhythmias. THE ABSOLUTE CLINICAL CONTRAINDICATION: BETA-BLOCKERS MUST NEVER BE INITIATED BEFORE EFFECTIVE ALPHA-BLOCKADE! Epinephrine and norepinephrine stimulate both alpha-1 (vasoconstriction) and beta-2 (vasodilation) receptors. If a beta-blocker is administered alone, beta-2 mediated vasodilation is abolished, leaving massive circulating catecholamines to stimulate alpha-1 receptors entirely UNOPPOSED. This triggers a catastrophic, life-threatening hypertensive crisis, severe coronary vasospasm, myocardial infarction, and acute pulmonary edema.

subject: Medicine
topic: Primary Hyperaldosteronism Screening Aldosterone-Renin Ratio and Sampling
stem: A 56-year-old man presents for evaluation of difficult-to-control hypertension. Despite full-dose therapy with amlodipine 10 mg daily, losartan 100 mg daily, and chlorthalidone 25 mg daily, his blood pressure remains elevated at 168/102 mm Hg. He reports mild muscle weakness and intermittent cramps but denies headache, palpitations, or diaphoresis. Physical examination shows no cushingoid features, abdominal bruits, or peripheral edema. Laboratory evaluation reveals: - Serum Sodium: 144 mEq/L - Serum Potassium: 2.9 mEq/L (unprovoked hypokalemia) - Serum Bicarbonate: 32 mEq/L (metabolic alkalosis) - Serum Creatinine: 1.0 mg/dL After correcting hypokalemia and withdrawing interfering medications, screening demonstrates: - Morning Plasma Aldosterone Concentration (PAC): 34 ng/dL (normal: 3-16 ng/dL) - Plasma Renin Activity (PRA): 0.6 ng/mL/hr (normal: 1-4 ng/mL/hr) - PAC/PRA Ratio: 56.7 (abnormal > 20) A confirmatory intravenous saline suppression test demonstrates a post-infusion PAC of 22 ng/dL (normal suppression: < 5 ng/dL). An abdominal CT scan reveals a 1.2-cm hypodense nodule in the left adrenal gland; the right adrenal gland appears minimally bulky. The patient is eager to undergo surgery to cure his hypertension. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management prior to surgical resection?

options.text: Perform bilateral adrenal vein sampling (AVS) to differentiate unilateral aldosterone hypersecretion from bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia
options.explanation: This patient presents with classic PRIMARY HYPERALDOSTERONISM (Conn syndrome), suggested by resistant hypertension on three antihypertensive medications, spontaneous hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and a positive screening PAC/PRA ratio > 20 with PAC > 15 ng/dL, confirmed by non-suppression on saline loading. SUBTYPE EVALUATION AND THE CRITICAL MANDATE FOR ADRENAL VEIN SAMPLING (AVS): Primary hyperaldosteronism is caused by either: (1) A unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma (APA; ~35% of cases), which is cured by laparoscopic unilateral adrenalectomy; or (2) Bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia (IAH; ~60% of cases), which does NOT benefit from surgery and must be managed medically with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone or eplerenone). High-resolution thin-section CT scanning of the adrenals is performed initially to rule out large adrenocortical carcinomas. HOWEVER, CT HAS SEVERE LIMITATIONS IN DIFFERENTIATING APA FROM IAH: Non-functioning benign adrenal cortical incidentalomas occur in up to 5% to 10% of individuals over age 40. A unilateral nodule on CT may be an innocent non-functioning incidentaloma, while the real source of aldosterone excess is micro-nodular hyperplasia in the opposite adrenal or bilateral glands. Conversely, small functional microadenomas (< 1 cm) are frequently missed on CT. ACCORDING TO ENDOCRINE SOCIETY GUIDELINES: In any candidate for surgery who is over 35 years of age, BILATERAL ADRENAL VEIN SAMPLING (AVS) IS ABSOLUTELY MANDATORY prior to surgical intervention. AVS is the undisputed gold standard for lateralization: Catheters measure cortisol-corrected aldosterone concentrations in both the right and left adrenal veins. A unilateral gradient (aldosterone/cortisol ratio > 4:1 compared to the contralateral side) confirms unilateral adenoma and predicts surgical cure by adrenalectomy. Lack of lateralization confirms bilateral hyperplasia, sparing the patient an unnecessary and futile unilateral adrenalectomy.

options.text: Proceed directly to laparoscopic left adrenalectomy based on the definitive CT visualization of the 1.2-cm nodule
options.explanation: CT cannot distinguish non-functioning incidentalomas from bilateral hyperplasia; operating without AVS risks removing a non-functional gland.

options.text: Perform bilateral renal vein renin sampling to evaluate for unilateral renal artery stenosis
options.explanation: Renal artery stenosis causes secondary hyperaldosteronism with elevated renin; primary hyperaldosteronism features suppressed renin (PRA 0.6).

options.text: Initiate high-dose furosemide monotherapy to promote urinary sodium excretion and manage hypertension
options.explanation: Loop diuretics further worsen hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis without addressing autonomous aldosterone receptor activation.

options.text: Reassure the patient and discontinue all medications, as unprovoked hypokalemia is a benign incidental finding
options.explanation: Untreated primary hyperaldosteronism leads to progressive myocardial fibrosis, stroke, ventricular arrhythmias, and end-stage renal disease.

topic: Cushing Syndrome Stepwise Diagnostic Algorithm and High-Dose Dexamethasone
stem: A 44-year-old woman presents to the clinic with progressive weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising, facial fullness, and irregular menses over the past 9 months. Her past medical history is notable for newly diagnosed hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Physical examination demonstrates plethoric rounded 'moon facies', dorsocervical fat pad ('buffalo hump'), central adiposity with thin extremities, and wide (> 1 cm), violaceous striae across her lower abdomen. Initial screening for hypercortisolism is markedly abnormal: - 24-hour urinary free cortisol: 340 mcg/24 hr (normal: < 50 mcg/24 hr) - Late-night salivary cortisol: 0.62 mcg/dL (normal: < 0.10 mcg/dL) - Overnight 1-mg low-dose dexamethasone suppression test: 8:00 AM serum cortisol is 14 mcg/dL (normal: < 1.8 mcg/dL) Subsequent evaluation reveals a morning plasma ACTH level of 68 pg/mL (normal: 10-60 pg/mL; inappropriately elevated ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome). The physician orders a high-dose (8-mg) overnight dexamethasone suppression test, which demonstrates a 72% suppression of morning serum cortisol compared to baseline. A pituitary MRI shows a 4-mm hypoenhancing microadenoma in the anterior pituitary. Which of the following is the definitive diagnosis and pathophysiological explanation for the high-dose dexamethasone test result?

options.text: Ectopic ACTH-secreting small cell lung carcinoma; neuroendocrine tumor cells possess upregulated glucocorticoid receptors that hyper-respond to high-dose dexamethasone
options.explanation: Ectopic ACTH-secreting tumors are autonomous and do NOT suppress with high-dose dexamethasone; > 50% suppression indicates pituitary Cushing disease.

options.text: Cushing disease (pituitary ACTH-secreting corticotroph adenoma); the neoplastic pituitary cells retain partial glucocorticoid negative feedback sensitivity, resulting in > 50% suppression with high-dose dexamethasone
options.explanation: This patient presents with clinical and biochemical evidence of CUSHING SYNDROME (hypercortisolemia), characterized by centripetal obesity, moon facies, buffalo hump, proximal muscle weakness, wide purple abdominal striae, and impaired glucose tolerance. Master the three-step diagnostic evaluation: (1) STEP 1 — CONFIRM HYPERCORTISOLEMIA: Endocrine Society guidelines require >= 2 concordant first-line tests: 24-hour urinary free cortisol (> 3x normal), late-night salivary cortisol (loss of nocturnal circadian nadir), or low-dose (1-mg) overnight dexamethasone suppression test (failure to suppress cortisol < 1.8 mcg/dL). This patient has three concordant positive tests, establishing pathological endogenous hypercortisolemia. (2) STEP 2 — DETERMINE ACTH DEPENDENCE: Plasma ACTH is measured: (a) If ACTH is suppressed (< 5 pg/mL), it is ACTH-INDEPENDENT Cushing syndrome (primary autonomous adrenal adenoma or carcinoma), worked up with an adrenal CT scan. (b) If ACTH is normal or elevated (>= 15-20 pg/mL), it is ACTH-DEPENDENT Cushing syndrome (driven by excess ACTH secretion). This patient ACTH is 68 pg/mL, confirming ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism. (3) STEP 3 — DIFFERENTIATE CUSHING DISEASE FROM ECTOPIC ACTH: The two causes of ACTH-dependent Cushing are: (a) CUSHING DISEASE (a benign ACTH-secreting pituitary corticotroph adenoma; accounts for ~80% of ACTH-dependent cases); and (b) ECTOPIC ACTH PRODUCTION (most commonly small cell lung carcinoma, bronchial carcinoid, or medullary thyroid carcinoma; accounts for ~20%). To differentiate them, the HIGH-DOSE (8-MG) DEXAMETHASONE SUPPRESSION TEST is performed: Pituitary corticotroph adenoma cells originate from normal pituitary cells and RETAIN PARTIAL SENSITIVITY TO NEGATIVE FEEDBACK INHIBITION; thus, massive supranormal doses of dexamethasone (8 mg) overcome the altered receptor threshold, causing a > 50% REDUCTION IN SERUM CORTISOL. In contrast, ectopic neuroendocrine tumors operate completely autonomously outside hypothalamic-pituitary control and exhibit ZERO suppression (< 50% drop). Definitive treatment for Cushing disease is transsphenoidal adenomectomy.

options.text: Primary autonomous adrenal cortical adenoma; high-dose dexamethasone directly inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase in the adrenal cortex
options.explanation: Adrenal adenomas produce ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome (ACTH < 5 pg/mL); this patient has elevated ACTH (68 pg/mL).

options.text: Exogenous factitious corticosteroid abuse; synthetic steroids suppress endogenous ACTH while cross-reacting in urinary free cortisol assays
options.explanation: Exogenous steroid ingestion suppresses endogenous ACTH and cortisol, resulting in low/undetectable plasma ACTH and cortisol levels.

options.text: Cyclical pseudo-Cushing syndrome secondary to major depressive disorder; high-dose dexamethasone normalizes hypothalamic CRH transcription
options.explanation: Pseudo-Cushing suppresses with low-dose dexamethasone (or combined dex-CRH); failure to suppress with 1-mg dex confirms true Cushing syndrome.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is admitted to the neurointensive care unit following surgical clipping of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm that ruptured 5 days ago, causing subarachnoid hemorrhage (Hunt and Hess grade II). Over the past 24 hours, she has become increasingly lethargic and confused. topic: Central vs Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus Water Deprivation Test Challenge
stem: A 46-year-old man with a 15-year history of bipolar I disorder treated with lithium carbonate presents to the outpatient clinic reporting constant thirst, frequent awakening at night to urinate (nocturia 4 to 5 times), and daily urine output exceeding 6 liters. He drinks large volumes of ice-cold water throughout the day. Physical examination reveals an alert man with dry mucous membranes and normal vital signs. Laboratory evaluation reveals: - Serum Sodium: 147 mEq/L - Serum Potassium: 4.0 mEq/L - Serum Creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL - Serum Glucose: 92 mg/dL - Serum Osmolality: 304 mOsm/kg (normal: 275-295 mOsm/kg) - Urine Osmolality: 120 mOsm/kg (inappropriately dilute) The patient is admitted for a supervised water deprivation test. After 8 hours of water deprivation, his serum osmolality rises to 312 mOsm/kg, and his serum sodium is 150 mEq/L; his urine osmolality remains low at 145 mOsm/kg. He is then administered 2 mcg of subcutaneous desmopressin (DDAVP). Two hours after desmopressin administration, his urine osmolality is 162 mOsm/kg (an increase of only 11.7%). Which of the following is the definitive diagnosis, and what is the most appropriate pharmacological management?

options.text: Central diabetes insipidus secondary to hypothalamic sarcoidosis; management requires lifelong therapy with intranasal desmopressin (DDAVP)
options.explanation: Central DI exhibits a dramatic > 50% to 100% surge in urine osmolality following desmopressin; failure to respond confirms nephrogenic DI.

options.text: Primary psychogenic polydipsia; management requires strict behavioral water restriction and psychiatric antipsychotic adjustment
options.explanation: In psychogenic polydipsia, water deprivation alone causes endogenous ADH release that successfully concentrates urine to > 600 mOsm/kg.

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH); management requires high-dose loop diuretics and oral demeclocycline
options.explanation: SIADH causes concentrated urine (> 100-300 mOsm/kg) and hyponatremia; this patient has dilute urine (145 mOsm/kg) and hypernatremia.

options.text: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus secondary to chronic lithium toxicity; management includes stopping lithium if feasible, initiating a low-sodium diet, and prescribing a thiazide diuretic or amiloride
options.explanation: This patient presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and severe urinary concentrating impairment on chronic lithium therapy. Master the diagnostic interpretation of the WATER DEPRIVATION AND DDAVP CHALLENGE TEST on USMLE Step 2 CK: (1) ESTABLISHING DIABETES INSIPIDUS (DI): When a normal individual is deprived of water, rising plasma osmolality stimulates hypothalamic osmoreceptors to release endogenous vasopressin (ADH), which inserts aquaporin-2 water channels into collecting duct principal cells, concentrating urine to > 600 to 800 mOsm/kg. In this patient, despite hyperosmolality (plasma Osm 312 mOsm/kg), urine remains dilute (145 mOsm/kg), confirming Diabetes Insipidus (inability to concentrate urine). (2) DIFFERENTIATING CENTRAL VS NEPHROGENIC DI (DDAVP RESPONSE): (a) In CENTRAL DI (lack of pituitary ADH secretion due to trauma, surgery, or idiopathic damage), the collecting duct receptors are completely normal. Administration of exogenous DDAVP triggers a DRAMATIC INCREASE IN URINE OSMOLALITY (typically > 50% to > 100% increase), often exceeding 400 to 600 mOsm/kg. (b) In NEPHROGENIC DI (end-organ renal unresponsiveness to ADH), collecting duct principal cells cannot respond to ADH. Administration of exogenous DDAVP produces MINIMAL OR ZERO RESPONSE (urine osmolality increases by < 50% or < 100 mOsm/kg). This patient rise from 145 to 162 mOsm/kg (an 11.7% increase) definitively confirms NEPHROGENIC DI. (3) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF LITHIUM-INDUCED NEPHROGENIC DI: Lithium enters collecting duct principal cells through the Epithelial Sodium Channel (ENaC), accumulating intracellularly and inhibiting glycogen synthase kinase-3beta (GSK-3beta) and adenylate cyclase, thereby blocking ADH-mediated aquaporin-2 gene transcription and translocation. (4) PHARMACOLOGICAL MANAGEMENT OF NEPHROGENIC DI: Desmopressin is ineffective. Management includes: (a) Discontinuing lithium if safe psychiatric alternatives exist; (b) Low-sodium and low-protein diet (decreases solute load delivery to the nephron); (c) THIAZIDE DIURETICS (such as hydrochlorothiazide): Thiazides inhibit distal Na-Cl cotransporters, producing mild volume depletion that drives compensatory proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption, reducing volume delivery to the collecting ducts and decreasing urine output; and (d) AMILORIDE: Specifically blocks ENaC, preventing further lithium entry and accumulation into collecting duct cells.

options.text: Type 4 renal tubular acidosis; management requires sodium bicarbonate infusion and oral fludrocortisone
options.explanation: Type 4 RTA presents with hyperkalemic normal anion gap metabolic acidosis in diabetic nephropathy, not profound polyuria with dilute urine.

subject: Surgery
topic: Hypocalcemia Post-Thyroidectomy and Intravenous Calcium Gluconate
stem: A 48-year-old woman is evaluated in the post-surgical step-down unit 36 hours after undergoing an uncomplicated total thyroidectomy and central neck lymph node dissection for a 3.5-cm papillary thyroid carcinoma. Over the past 4 hours, she has experienced progressive perioral tingling, numbness in her fingertips, and severe bilateral hand cramping. On physical examination, she is anxious and diaphoretic. Vital signs are: temperature 37.1 C, pulse 84/min, blood pressure 132/82 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 18/min. Surgical neck incision is clean, dry, and intact without hematoma, swelling, or stridor. Tapping gently over the trunk of the facial nerve immediately anterior to the left external auditory meatus elicits involuntary twitching of the left upper lip and alae nasi (positive Chvostek sign). Inflation of a blood pressure cuff on her right arm to 150 mm Hg (20 mm Hg above her systolic pressure) for 2 minutes induces painful carpopedal spasm characterized by flexion of the wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints, extension of the interphalangeal joints, and adduction of the thumb ('obstetrician's hand', positive Trousseau sign). A 12-lead ECG demonstrates sinus rhythm with marked prolongation of the corrected QT interval (QTc = 510 ms). Stat laboratory testing reveals: total serum calcium 6.6 mg/dL (normal: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL), serum albumin 4.0 g/dL, and ionized calcium 0.82 mmol/L (normal: 1.15-1.33 mmol/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacotherapeutic intervention?

options.text: Intravenous calcium chloride 10% bolus rapidly pushed through a peripheral forearm intravenous line
options.explanation: Calcium chloride causes severe peripheral chemical thrombophlebitis and full-thickness cutaneous necrosis if extravasated; calcium gluconate is preferred.

options.text: Oral ergocalciferol (vitamin D2) 50,000 IU daily monotherapy with discharge home and follow-up in 2 weeks
options.explanation: Ergocalciferol requires PTH-dependent renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation and takes weeks to act; acute tetany requires immediate IV calcium gluconate.

options.text: Intravenous potassium chloride infusion combined with oral magnesium oxide to correct hypomagnesemic tetany
options.explanation: The primary defect is documented severe hypocalcemia; potassium does not correct hypocalcemic tetany or QT prolongation.

options.text: Emergency surgical exploration of the neck incision under general anesthesia to evacuate a compressive wound hematoma
options.explanation: Wound hematoma presents with rapid neck swelling, tracheal deviation, and respiratory stridor, not tetany or prolonged QT intervals.

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate infusion with continuous cardiac monitoring, followed by oral calcium carbonate and active calcitriol
options.explanation: This patient presents with acute, severe, symptomatic HYPOCALCEMIA following total thyroidectomy. Master the pathophysiology, physical diagnosis, and management tested on USMLE Step 2 CK: (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Total thyroidectomy carries a 10% to 30% risk of transient hypoparathyroidism (and a 1% to 3% risk of permanent hypoparathyroidism) due to mechanical trauma, devascularization, or accidental excision of the delicate parathyroid glands. Because parathyroid hormone (PTH) has a short half-life (3 to 5 minutes), PTH levels plunge immediately post-surgery, with serum calcium falling to a nadir 24 to 48 hours postoperatively as bone and soft-tissue calcium buffers equilibrate. (2) NEUROMUSCULAR SYMPTOMS AND PHYSICAL SIGNS: Extracellular calcium normally stabilizes axonal membrane potentials by modulating voltage-gated sodium channels. Hypocalcemia increases neuronal membrane permeability to sodium, lowering the threshold for axonal depolarization and producing hyperreflexia and tetany: (a) Sensory paresthesias: Perioral numbness and tingling of fingers and toes; (b) Motor hyperexcitability: Muscle spasms, carpopedal spasm, and life-threatening laryngospasm/bronchospasm; (c) CHVOSTEK SIGN: Percussion of the facial nerve at the angle of the jaw elicits twitching of facial muscles; (d) TROUSSEAU SIGN: Sphygmomanometer cuff inflation above systolic pressure for 3 minutes induces painful carpopedal spasm (positive in >90% of hypocalcemic patients, substantially more sensitive and specific than Chvostek sign). (3) ECG FINDINGS: Hypocalcemia prolongs phase 2 of the cardiac action potential, manifesting as PROLONGATION OF THE ST SEGMENT AND CORRECTED QT INTERVAL (QTc), predisposing to torsades de pointes ventricular tachycardia. (4) EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT: Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia is a medical emergency. The treatment of choice is INTRAVENOUS CALCIUM GLUCONATE (1 to 2 grams of 10% calcium gluconate infused over 10 to 20 minutes) with continuous cardiac telemetry. Calcium gluconate is strongly preferred over intravenous calcium chloride because calcium chloride is three times more hyperosmolar and causes severe, blistering chemical thrombophlebitis and full-thickness cutaneous necrosis if peripheral extravasation occurs. Once acute symptoms are controlled, the patient is transitioned to oral calcium carbonate and active vitamin D (CALCITRIOL, 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol) because endogenous PTH is deficient to activate 1-alpha-hydroxylase.

topic: Severe Hypercalcemia Crisis Aggressive Saline and Zoledronic Acid
stem: A 64-year-old woman with metastatic squamous cell lung carcinoma presents to the emergency department with profound lethargy, confusion, nausea, severe constipation, and generalized abdominal pain for 3 days. Her daughter reports she has been drinking copious amounts of water and urinating constantly. On physical examination, she is obtunded, responding only to loud verbal stimuli with garbled speech. Physical examination reveals deeply sunken orbits, dry parched tongue, flat neck veins, and poor skin turgor. Vital signs are: temperature 37.0 C, pulse 116/min, supine blood pressure 92/56 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 16/min. Neurological examination reveals generalized hyporeflexia and profound proximal muscle weakness without focal deficits. A 12-lead ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia with a shortened corrected QT interval (QTc = 340 ms). Laboratory evaluation reveals: - Total Serum Calcium: 15.2 mg/dL (normal: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL) - Serum Albumin: 3.2 g/dL (Corrected Calcium = 15.8 mg/dL) - Serum Phosphorus: 1.8 mg/dL (normal: 2.5-4.5 mg/dL) - Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN): 54 mg/dL - Serum Creatinine: 2.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL 1 month ago) - Intact Parathyroid Hormone (PTH): Suppressed at 4 pg/mL (normal: 10-65 pg/mL) Which of the following sequences represents the most appropriate, guideline-adherent initial management strategy for this patient?

options.text: Aggressive intravenous volume resuscitation with 0.9% normal saline, combined with subcutaneous calcitonin for rapid calcium reduction and intravenous zoledronic acid for durable osteoclast inhibition
options.explanation: This patient presents with a severe HYPERCALCEMIC CRISIS secondary to hypercalcemia of malignancy (humoral hypercalcemia mediated by PTH-related peptide [PTHrP] from squamous cell lung carcinoma, causing hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and suppressed intact PTH). Serum calcium > 14 mg/dL represents a life-threatening oncologic emergency requiring immediate multimodal management: (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF SEVERE DEHYDRATION: Hypercalcemia induces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by activating calcium-sensing receptors (CaSR) in the thick ascending limb and collecting ducts, impairing aquaporin-2 water channel insertion and causing massive polyuria, urinary sodium wasting, and total-body volume depletion (often 4 to 6 liters deficient). Severe hypovolemia reduces glomerular filtration rate (GFR), diminishing renal calcium excretion and creating a lethal positive feedback loop of accelerating hypercalcemia and acute prerenal azotemia. (2) THREE-STEP PHARMACOLOGICAL PROTOCOL: (a) STEP 1 (IMMEDIATE): AGGRESSIVE INTRAVENOUS ISOTONIC (0.9%) NORMAL SALINE RESUSCITATION. Infuse 200 to 300 mL/hr (after an initial 1-2 L bolus) to expand intravascular volume, restore renal blood flow, increase GFR, and enhance proximal tubular sodium and calcium excretion. stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 1-week history of severe anterior neck pain that radiates upward to her jaw and ears. She reports palpitations, anxiety, heat intolerance, diaphoresis, and fine tremors over the past 4 days. She notes that 3 weeks ago, she had an uncomplicated viral upper respiratory tract infection characterized by rhinorrhea, sore throat, and low-grade fevers that resolved spontaneously. On physical examination, she appears anxious and restless. Vital signs are: temperature 38.1 C, pulse 108/min, and blood pressure 138/78 mm Hg. Palpation of the anterior neck reveals an exquisitely tender, symmetrically enlarged, firm, nodule-free thyroid gland; light palpation elicits severe discomfort. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy, and eye examination demonstrates no exophthalmos, lid lag, or proptosis. Laboratory evaluation reveals: - Serum TSH: < 0.01 microU/mL (normal: 0.4-4.0 microU/mL) - Free T4: 3.2 ng/dL (normal: 0.8-1.8 ng/dL) - Total T3: 240 ng/dL (normal: 80-200 ng/dL) - Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR): 94 mm/hr (normal: < 20 mm/hr) - C-Reactive Protein (CRP): 48 mg/L (normal: < 5 mg/L) - Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulin (TSI): Negative - Anti-Thyroid Peroxidase (anti-TPO) Antibodies: Negative A 24-hour radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) scan demonstrates a diffuse uptake of only 0.8% (normal: 10% to 30%). Which of the following is the most appropriate management strategy for this patient?

options.text: Initiate oral methimazole 20 mg daily to inhibit thyroid peroxidase and suppress thyroid hormone organification
options.explanation: Methimazole blocks new hormone synthesis; in subacute thyroiditis, hyperthyroidism is caused by passive leak of preformed hormone, rendering methimazole useless.

options.text: Initiate high-dose oral ibuprofen (or oral prednisone for severe refractory pain) combined with oral propranolol for adrenergic symptoms; thionamides are completely ineffective
options.explanation: This patient presents with classic SUBACUTE GRANULOMATOUS THYROIDITIS (also known as de Quervain thyroiditis or painful subacute thyroiditis). Master the clinical hallmarks, diagnostic testing, and pharmacological rationale on USMLE Step 2 CK: (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND CLINICAL PRESENTATION: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is a post-viral inflammatory reaction (most commonly following upper respiratory infection with Coxsackievirus, adenovirus, mumps, echovirus, or influenza). It classically occurs in young to middle-aged women presenting with an EXQUISITELY PAINFUL, TENDER THYROID GOITER with pain characteristically radiating upward to the angle of the jaw, earlobes, or occiput, accompanied by fever and fatigue. Histopathology demonstrates granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and follicular disruption. (2) THREE-PHASE CLINICAL COURSE: (a) Hyperthyroid Phase (lasts 2 to 6 weeks): Inflammatory destruction of follicular basement membranes causes passive leak of preformed, stored thyroglobulin, T4, and T3 into the circulation. (b) Hypothyroid Phase (lasts weeks to months): Stored hormone is exhausted, and the inflamed thyroid tissue cannot synthesize new hormones. (c) Recovery Phase: Follicular architecture regenerates, and >95% of patients return to a normal euthyroid state within 6 to 12 months. (3) THE DIAGNOSTIC TRIAD: (a) Suppressed TSH with elevated free T4/T3; (b) DRAMATICALLY ELEVATED INFLAMMATORY MARKERS (ESR often > 80 to 100 mm/hr, elevated CRP); and (c) MARKEDLY SUPPRESSED RADIOACTIVE IODINE UPTAKE (RAIU < 1% to 3%). In Graves disease, RAIU is diffusely ELEVATED (40% to 70%) because hyperfunctioning follicular cells actively synthesize thyroid hormone. In subacute thyroiditis, the inflamed, damaged follicular cells are completely incapable of trapping radioactive iodine. (4) PHARMACOTHERAPY AND THE THIONAMIDE PITFALL: Management is purely supportive: HIGH-DOSE NONSTEROIDAL ANTI-INFLAMMATORY DRUGS (NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID) are the first-line therapy to relieve neck pain and inflammation. In patients with severe, unremitting pain or high fevers, ORAL PREDNISONE (40 mg daily tapered over 4 to 6 weeks) provides dramatic symptom relief within 24 to 48 hours. Palpitations and tremor are controlled with a BETA-BLOCKER (propranolol). CRITICAL CONTRAINDICATION: THIONAMIDES (METHIMAZOLE OR PROPYLTHIOURACIL) ARE ENTIRELY INEFFECTIVE! Thionamides act by inhibiting thyroid peroxidase to block de novo thyroid hormone synthesis. Because thyrotoxicosis in de Quervain thyroiditis is caused by the passive leak of preformed hormone from ruptured follicles rather than new hormone synthesis, thionamides provide zero clinical benefit and expose the patient to unnecessary toxicities.

options.text: Administer therapeutic radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation to destroy hyperactive thyroid follicular cells
options.explanation: The thyroid gland has an RAIU of only 0.8% and cannot absorb therapeutic radioactive iodine; I-131 is completely ineffective and contraindicated.

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for 14 days to treat acute suppurative bacterial thyroiditis
options.explanation: Acute suppurative thyroiditis is a rare bacterial infection presenting with a focal unilateral fluctuant abscess, high fever, and leukocytosis, not diffuse de Quervain thyroiditis.

options.text: Perform emergent total thyroidectomy to eliminate the risk of transformation into anaplastic thyroid carcinoma
options.explanation: Subacute thyroiditis is a self-limiting benign condition with spontaneous resolution in >95% of cases; surgical thyroidectomy is contraindicated.

stem: An 18-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after experiencing a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. His past medical history is notable for recurrent, severe oral and esophageal thrush requiring repeated courses of oral fluconazole since age 3, as well as dystrophic, ridged, pitted fingernails and dental enamel hypoplasia. At age 9, he was diagnosed with primary hypoparathyroidism presenting with carpopedal spasms and hypocalcemia, maintained on oral calcium and calcitriol. Over the past 3 months, he has developed progressive fatigue, anorexia, dizzy spells upon standing, salt cravings, and dark hyperpigmentation of his palmar creases and gums. On physical examination, he is postictal but arousable. Vital signs are: temperature 37.0 C, pulse 94/min, supine blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg, and standing blood pressure 76/44 mm Hg with dizziness. Physical examination demonstrates confluent white plaques on the buccal mucosa, diffuse hyperpigmentation, patchy alopecia areata of the scalp, and a positive Chvostek sign. Emergency laboratory testing reveals: - Serum Calcium: 6.8 mg/dL (normal: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL) - Serum Phosphorus: 5.6 mg/dL (normal: 2.5-4.5 mg/dL) - Intact Parathyroid Hormone (PTH): 6 pg/mL (inappropriately low) - Serum Sodium: 126 mEq/L - Serum Potassium: 5.6 mEq/L - Blood Urea Nitrogen: 32 mg/dL - Morning Serum Cortisol: 2.1 mcg/dL - Plasma ACTH: 280 pg/mL (markedly elevated) Which of the following genetic defects and clinical syndromes is primarily responsible for this patient multi-system disorder?

options.text: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 2 (Schmidt syndrome) caused by polygenic inheritance linked to HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 alleles
options.explanation: APS-2 features Addison disease with autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes; it never presents with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis or hypoparathyroidism.

options.text: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome) resulting in defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches
options.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome causes hypocalcemia and T-cell deficiency, but presents in infancy with conotruncal cardiac anomalies, cleft palate, and dysmorphic facies, without Addison disease.

options.text: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) caused by an autosomal recessive mutation in the AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) gene
options.explanation: This patient presents with the full classic clinical triad of AUTOIMMUNE POLYGLANDULAR SYNDROME TYPE 1 (APS-1), also known as Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED) or Whitaker syndrome. Master the genetics, immunology, and clinical distinctions on USMLE Step 2 CK: (1) GENETICS AND IMMUNOLOGICAL MECHANISM: APS-1 is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) GENE on chromosome 21q22. The AIRE transcription factor is expressed in medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs), where it drives the promiscuous ectopic transcription of peripheral tissue-specific antigens (such as insulin, myelin basic protein, and steroidogenic enzymes). This presentation enables the NEGATIVE SELECTION (clonal deletion) of autoreactive developing T cells. In the absence of functional AIRE, autoreactive T-cell clones escape into the systemic circulation, launching multi-organ autoimmune attacks against endocrine glands and tissues. Patients also develop high-titer neutralizing autoantibodies against interleukin-17 (IL-17A, IL-17F) and interleukin-22, which impairs mucosal Th17-mediated immunity and accounts for susceptibility to persistent Candida infections. (2) CLASSIC DIAGNOSTIC TRIAD (PRESENTATION CHRONOLOGY): Diagnosis requires >= 2 of the following 3 major clinical manifestations: (a) CHRONIC MUCOCUTANEOUS CANDIDIASIS: The earliest manifestation, typically presenting in infancy or early childhood (< 5 years) with intractable oral, cutaneous, or ungual candidiasis; (b) AUTOIMMUNE HYPOPARATHYROIDISM: The most frequent endocrine manifestation (seen in ~80%), presenting in early childhood with hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, paresthesias, tetany, and seizures; and (c) PRIMARY ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY (Addison disease): Typically manifests in late childhood, adolescence, or early adulthood, presenting with fatigue, hyperpigmentation, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and adrenal crisis. Additional features include ectodermal dystrophy (dental enamel pitting, nail ridging), alopecia areata, vitiligo, primary hypogonadism, autoimmune hepatitis, and pernicious anemia. (3) CRITICAL CONTRAST WITH AUTOIMMUNE POLYGLANDULAR SYNDROME TYPE 2 (APS-2; Schmidt Syndrome): APS-2 is a polygenic, adult-onset disorder strongly associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 alleles. APS-2 is characterized by: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison disease) + Autoimmune Thyroid Disease (Hashimoto thyroiditis or Graves disease) + Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus. APS-2 NEVER FEATURES CHRONIC MUCOCUTANEOUS CANDIDIASIS OR HYPOPARATHYROIDISM.

options.explanation: MEN1 causes hyperparathyroidism (hypercalcemia), enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, and pituitary adenomas, not hypoparathyroidism or adrenal insufficiency.

options.text: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) caused by an X-linked mutation in the common gamma chain (IL2RG) gene
options.explanation: SCID presents in early infancy with failure to thrive and severe fatal opportunistic infections, not adult Addison disease or hypoparathyroidism.

topic: Acromegaly Screening Serum IGF-1 and Confirmatory Oral Glucose Challenge
stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the clinic with progressive fatigue, excessive sweating, joint aches, and bilateral hand numbness over the past 3 years. His wife notes that he has developed loud snoring and witnessed breath pauses during sleep. Over the past 5 years, he has had to purchase larger wedding rings twice (moving from ring size 9 to 12) and has gone from shoe size 10 to 12.5. Physical examination reveals an enlarged, broad skull with prominent supraorbital ridges (frontal bossing), an enlarged protruding lower jaw with widened dental spacing (prognathism), a thick fleshy nose, and a large tongue (macroglossia). His hands are wide and spade-like with moist palms. Neurological examination reveals bilateral positive Phalen and Tinel signs at the wrists consistent with carpal tunnel syndrome. Blood pressure is 154/96 mm Hg. Fasting blood glucose is 134 mg/dL. The physician suspects acromegaly. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial screening test, followed by the definitive confirmatory dynamic diagnostic test for this patient?

options.text: Measure random morning fasting serum growth hormone concentration, followed by an insulin-induced hypoglycemia challenge test
options.explanation: Random GH is pulsatile and unreliable for screening; insulin hypoglycemia tests for GH deficiency, not GH hypersecretion in acromegaly.

options.text: Perform a 24-hour urinary free cortisol test, followed by an overnight 8-mg high-dose dexamethasone suppression test
options.explanation: Urinary cortisol and dexamethasone tests evaluate Cushing syndrome, not growth hormone excess and acromegaly.

options.text: Order a non-contrast skull radiograph to evaluate sella turcica enlargement, followed by immediate initiation of oral cabergoline
options.explanation: Plain radiographs are obsolete; biochemical confirmation with IGF-1 and OGTT must precede neuroimaging and treatment.

options.explanation: This patient presents with classic, advanced ACROMEGALY, a systemic disorder resulting from chronic, excessive growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) hypersecretion, almost universally caused by a benign GH-secreting pituitary somatotroph adenoma (>75% of which are macroadenomas > 1 cm at diagnosis). Master the multi-step diagnostic algorithm established by Endocrine Society guidelines: (1) STEP 1 — INITIAL SCREENING TEST: The best initial screening test is measurement of SERUM INSULIN-LIKE GROWTH FACTOR-1 (IGF-1) CONCENTRATION (age- and sex-adjusted). Why not random Growth Hormone (GH)? GH is secreted by normal somatotrophs in sharp, episodic pulses (mainly nocturnal) with a circulating half-life of only ~20 minutes. Random GH measurements fluctuate wildly throughout the day from undetectable troughs (< 0.2 ng/mL) to sharp peaks following exercise, stress, or meals; thus, a single normal GH level cannot rule out acromegaly. In contrast, IGF-1 (synthesized primarily in the liver in response to GH) has a long circulating half-life (>15 hours) bound to IGF-binding protein 3, providing a stable, highly sensitive biological integrator of 24-hour GH activity. An elevated IGF-1 is virtually 100% sensitive for acromegaly. (2) STEP 2 — CONFIRMATORY DYNAMIC TESTING: If serum IGF-1 is elevated, the definitive confirmatory dynamic test is the ORAL GLUCOSE TOLERANCE TEST (OGTT) WITH SERIAL GH MEASUREMENTS. (3) STEP 3 — IMAGING AND DEFINITIVE THERAPY: Once biochemical confirmation is established, CONTRAST-ENHANCED PITUITARY MRI is performed for precise anatomical visualization and evaluation of optic chiasm compression. topic: Macroprolactinoma Hook Effect Dilution and First-Line Cabergoline
stem: A 52-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of worsening dull frontal headaches, progressive loss of peripheral vision, complete loss of libido, and inability to achieve penile erections. Physical examination reveals an alert man with normal vital signs. Formal visual field confrontation testing demonstrates dense bitemporal hemianopsia. Neurological examination reveals no cranial nerve palsies, and testicular examination reveals bilateral soft, small testes (volume 8 mL; normal: 15-25 mL). A contrast-enhanced brain and pituitary MRI reveals a 3.6-cm x 2.8-cm invasive pituitary macroadenoma extending superiorly into the suprasellar cistern, compressing the optic chiasm, and invading the left cavernous sinus. Diagnostic laboratory testing reveals: - Total Testosterone: 82 ng/dL (normal: 300-1,000 ng/dL) - Luteinizing Hormone (LH): 1.1 mIU/mL (inappropriately low) - Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH): 1.4 mIU/mL - Free T4: 0.9 ng/dL (normal) - 8:00 AM Cortisol: 12 mcg/dL (normal) - Serum Prolactin: 78 ng/dL (normal: 3-20 ng/dL) The neurosurgical team is consulted and proposes immediate emergent transsphenoidal craniotomy, assuming the mass is a non-functioning gonadotroph macroadenoma causing stalk compression hyperprolactinemia. However, the consulting endocrinologist suspects a laboratory artifact. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in laboratory evaluation, and what is the definitive first-line therapy if confirmed?

options.text: Proceed directly to emergent transsphenoidal surgical resection, as medical therapy is completely ineffective for macroadenomas exceeding 3 cm in diameter
options.explanation: Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) are the first-line treatment for all prolactinomas, shrinking >85% of macroprolactinomas and resolving visual field defects.

options.text: Measure serum monomeric vs macroprolactin concentrations using polyethylene glycol precipitation to confirm pseudoprolactinemia
options.explanation: Macroprolactinemia causes false high prolactin without symptoms; here, severe hypogonadism and a 3.6-cm tumor indicate true tumor excess with hook effect.

options.text: Initiate high-dose stereotactic fractionated radiosurgery followed by lifelong recombinant growth hormone replacement
options.explanation: Radiotherapy is third-line therapy reserved for refractory tumors failing surgery and medications; medical therapy with cabergoline is first-line.

options.text: Administer intramuscular testosterone replacement therapy monotherapy without addressing the pituitary mass
options.explanation: Testosterone monotherapy without addressing the macroadenoma will allow progressive chiasmal compression and permanent, irreversible blindness.

options.text: Request a repeat prolactin assay with 1:100 serial serum dilution to overcome the 'hook effect' artifact; if confirmed, first-line therapy is medical management with oral cabergoline
options.explanation: This patient presents with a giant pituitary macroadenoma (> 3 cm) producing chiasmal compression (bitemporal hemianopsia), secondary hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and a paradoxically modest prolactin elevation of 78 ng/mL. Master the diagnostic pitfall of the 'HOOK EFFECT' and prolactinoma management on USMLE Step 2 CK: (1) DIFFERENTIATING PROLACTINOMA FROM STALK EFFECT: Pituitary tumors elevate prolactin via two mechanisms: (a) TRUE PROLACTINOMAS: A prolactinoma secretes prolactin in direct proportion to tumor volume. A 3.5-cm macroprolactinoma virtually always produces serum prolactin levels > 1,000 to 10,000 ng/mL. (b) STALK COMPRESSION HYPERPROLACTINEMIA (THE 'STALK EFFECT'): Any non-functioning pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, or infundibular mass that compresses the pituitary stalk disrupts the descending dopaminergic inhibitory tone from the hypothalamus to normal lactotrophs. Loss of dopamine inhibition causes mild prolactin elevation (typically 20 to 100 ng/mL, almost never > 200 ng/mL). (2) THE 'HIGH-DOSE HOOK EFFECT' ARTIFACT: In modern laboratory testing, prolactin is measured using two-site two-antibody immunometric 'sandwich' assays. When a giant macroprolactinoma produces astronomical concentrations of prolactin (> 5,000-20,000 ng/mL), the massive abundance of circulating prolactin molecules saturates both the solid-phase capture antibodies and the soluble detection antibodies independently. This prevents the formation of the required capture-antibody/antigen/detection-antibody sandwich complexes, resulting in a paradoxically false, deceptively low signal (reported as 50 to 150 ng/mL). (3) OVERCOMING THE ARTIFACT: The clinician must request REPEAT TESTING WITH 1:100 SERIAL SERUM DILUTION. Dilution reduces the overwhelming antigen concentration, allowing proper sandwich formation and unmasking true prolactin levels exceeding 10,000 ng/mL, definitively establishing macroprolactinoma. (4) FIRST-LINE TREATMENT: PROLACTINOMAS ARE UNIQUE AMONG PITUITARY TUMORS: SURGERY IS NOT THE FIRST-LINE THERAPY, EVEN IN THE PRESENCE OF MACROADENOMAS AND VISUAL COMPROMISE! The first-line therapy is MEDICAL MANAGEMENT WITH DOPAMINE D2-RECEPTOR AGONISTS, specifically CABERGOLINE (preferred over bromocriptine due to higher efficacy, longer half-life, and superior tolerability). Cabergoline rapidly induces cellular shrinkage and tumor involution in >85% of macroprolactinomas, rapidly restoring visual fields within days to weeks and avoiding invasive neurosurgery.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Extremely high concentrations of antigen (prolactin > 5,000-10,000 ng/mL) saturate both the capture and detection antibodies in two-site immunometric assays simultaneously, preventing antibody-antigen-antibody sandwich formation! subject: Medicine
topic: Pituitary Apoplexy Stress Corticosteroids and Surgical Decompression
stem: A 56-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to the sudden onset of an excruciating, explosive retro-orbital headache that began 3 hours ago, accompanied by nausea, recurrent vomiting, and double vision. His past medical history is notable for mild erectile dysfunction and intermittent headaches over the past year for which he did not seek medical care. On physical examination, he is acutely ill, lethargic, and photophobic. Vital signs are: temperature 36.8 C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 84/52 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 20/min. Neuro-ophthalmologic examination reveals bilateral visual acuity reduction (20/200 bilaterally), dense bitemporal visual field loss on confrontation, and complete right ptosis with the right eye resting in a 'down-and-out' position with a dilated, non-reactive pupil (complete right cranial nerve III palsy). Neck stiffness is absent. Point-of-care fingerstick blood glucose is 58 mg/dL. An emergency non-contrast brain CT scan reveals an expanded sella turcica containing a 2.8-cm hyperdense mass with a fluid-debris level and suprasellar extension, compressing the optic chiasm, consistent with acute pituitary apoplexy. Which of the following is the most critical immediate pharmacotherapeutic intervention for this patient?

options.text: Immediate administration of intravenous stress-dose hydrocortisone (100 mg IV bolus followed by 100 mg every 8 hours) to prevent fatal secondary adrenal crisis
options.explanation: This patient presents with classic PITUITARY APOPLEXY, an acute, life-threatening neuroendocrine emergency characterized by rapid ischemic infarction or hemorrhagic necrosis of a pre-existing (and often unrecognized) pituitary adenoma: (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND TRIGGERS: Pituitary adenomas often outgrow their delicate hypophyseal portal vascular supply, creating intrinsic tissue ischemia and high intrasellar pressures. Precipitants include systemic arterial hypertension, major cardiac surgery, coagulation disorders, anticoagulation, or initiation of dopamine agonists. (2) CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: (a) Severe 'thunderclap' headache: Sudden, excruciating retro-orbital, frontal, or holocranial pain caused by acute stretching of the dura mater and sellar diaphragma; (b) Visual loss and bitemporal hemianopsia: Caused by acute superior expansion compressing the overlying optic chiasm; (c) Acute cavernous sinus compression / ophthalmoplegia: Lateral expansion compresses cranial nerves running through the cavernous sinus (CN III, IV, and VI). Cranial nerve III (oculomotor) is most vulnerable, causing ptosis, 'down-and-out' eye deviation, and mydriasis; (d) LIFE-THREATENING ACUTE SECONDARY ADRENAL COLLAPSE: This is the primary cause of acute mortality in pituitary apoplexy. Rapid hemorrhagic destruction of anterior pituitary corticotrophs causes immediate cessation of ACTH release, leading to profound acute glucocorticoid deficiency. Patients present with refractory hypotension, circulatory shock, hypoglycemia, and altered mental status. (3) CRITICAL MANAGEMENT PRIORITIES: (a) STEP 1 (IMMEDIATE LIFE-SAVING ACTION): INTRAVENOUS STRESS-DOSE GLUCOCORTICOIDS (hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat, followed by 100 mg IV every 8 hours). Corticosteroid replacement must NEVER be delayed for endocrine testing or imaging! Initiating hydrocortisone stabilizes vasomotor tone, treats acute adrenal collapse, and reduces sellar edema. (b) STEP 2: Emergency MRI of the pituitary (superior to CT for delineating hemorrhage vs infarction and optic chiasm compression). (c) STEP 3: URGENT TRANSSPHENOIDAL SURGICAL DECOMPRESSION: Indicated for patients with severe or deteriorating visual acuity, progressive visual field loss, or declining level of consciousness. Patients with stable mild deficits can occasionally be managed conservatively with close neuro-ophthalmologic monitoring.

options.text: Immediate transfer to the operating room for emergency craniotomy, withholding glucocorticoids until intraoperative pituitary tissue biopsies are secured
options.explanation: Withholding glucocorticoid replacement in acute pituitary apoplexy leads to fatal intraoperative circulatory collapse from acute secondary adrenal failure.

options.text: Intravenous mannitol infusion combined with hyperventilation to lower intracranial pressure before performing digital subtraction cerebral angiography
options.explanation: The primary pathology is intrasellar hemorrhage and adrenal collapse; angiography is indicated for aneurysms, but apoplexy mandates hydrocortisone.

options.text: Initiation of high-dose oral cabergoline via nasogastric tube to induce rapid pituitary tumor shrinkage
options.explanation: Dopamine agonists can actually precipitate pituitary apoplexy and are contraindicated during acute hemorrhagic necrosis.

options.text: Intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) infusion to dissolve intrasellar microvascular thrombi
options.explanation: Administering tPA in acute pituitary hemorrhagic infarction causes catastrophic, fatal intracranial hemorrhage.

subject: Medicine
topic: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 RET Gene and Medullary Carcinoma
stem: A 19-year-old tall, slender man is evaluated in the endocrine genetics clinic. He has a long history of bumpy lips and tongue since childhood. Over the past 6 months, he has noticed a firm, painless swelling in the right side of his neck, as well as intermittent episodes of pounding headaches, diaphoresis, and palpitations. On physical examination, he has an asthenic, Marfanoid habitus with long, thin limbs, joint hyperlaxity, and a high-arched palate, but no lens subluxation or aortic root dilation on echocardiography. Multiple soft, fleshy, pedunculated nodules are present along the anterior vermilion border of his lips, dorsal tongue, and eyelid margins (mucosal neuromas). Neck examination demonstrates a hard, fixed, 3-cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe with palpable ipsilateral jugular lymphadenopathy. Blood pressure is 164/102 mm Hg, and pulse is 108/min. Laboratory evaluation reveals: - Serum Calcitonin: 1,480 pg/mL (normal: < 10 pg/mL) - Serum Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA): 84 ng/mL (normal: < 3 ng/mL) - 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines: Markedly elevated - Serum Calcium: 9.4 mg/dL (normal: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL) - Intact Parathyroid Hormone: 32 pg/mL (normal: 10-65 pg/mL) A fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid nodule confirms medullary thyroid carcinoma with amyloid deposition on Congo red staining. Which of the following genetic alterations and syndromes is the underlying cause of this patient condition?

options.text: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1) caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11
options.explanation: MEN1 causes parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors (the 3 Ps); it never features medullary thyroid carcinoma, mucosal neuromas, or pheochromocytoma.

options.text: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2B (MEN2B) caused by a germline gain-of-function point mutation in the RET proto-oncogene
options.explanation: This patient presents with the classic phenotype of MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 2B (MEN2B), characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytoma (headaches, palpitations, elevated metanephrines), mucosal neuromas, and a Marfanoid habitus. Master the genetics and clinical distinctions between MEN syndromes on USMLE Step 2 CK: (1) GENETICS OF MEN2: Both MEN2A and MEN2B are autosomal dominant syndromes caused by germline GAIN-OF-FUNCTION MUTATIONS IN THE RET PROTO-ONCOGENE on chromosome 10q11.2. The RET gene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in neural crest cellular signaling. In MEN2B, >95% of cases are caused by a specific point mutation (M918T in exon 16). (2) COMPARISON OF MEN SYNDROMES: (a) MEN TYPE 1 (Wermer Syndrome; MEN1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11, encoding Menin): Characterized by the '3 Ps': Parathyroid hyperplasia (hypercalcemia in >95%), Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma, insulinoma, VIPoma), and Pituitary adenomas (prolactinoma). (b) MEN TYPE 2A (Sipple Syndrome): Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (>95%) + Pheochromocytoma (50%) + Parathyroid Hyperplasia (20-30%). (c) MEN TYPE 2B: Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (>95%) + Pheochromocytoma (50%) + Mucosal Neuromas (ganglioneuromas of lips, tongue, eyelids, and intestine causing chronic constipation/megacolon) + Marfanoid habitus (arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum, joint laxity). CRITICAL DISTINCTION: PARATHYROID HYPERPLASIA IS ABSENT IN MEN2B! (3) CLINICAL BEHAVIOR OF MEDULLARY THYROID CARCINOMA: MTC is derived from neuroendocrine parafollicular C cells of the thyroid that secrete CALCITONIN. Histology shows sheets of polygonal cells in an AMYLOID STROMA (composed of calcitonin fibrils that stain positive with Congo red showing apple-green birefringence). Serum calcitonin and CEA serve as tumor markers. MTC in MEN2B is extraordinarily aggressive, developing in infancy and metastasizing early to regional lymph nodes and viscera. (4) SURGICAL SEQUENCE: If a patient has both pheochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma, THE PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA MUST BE RESECTED FIRST (after adequate alpha-blockade) to avoid fatal hypertensive crisis during thyroid surgery!

options.text: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2A (MEN2A) caused by an inactivating mutation in the calcium-sensing receptor (CASR) gene
